source.title: Provable Benefits of Overparameterization in Model Compression: From Double Descent to Pruning Neural Networks
source.authors: Xiang-Yu Chang; Ying-Cong Li; Samet Oymak; Christos Thrampoulidis

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model width and reports test-risk behavior, but uses a pruning-and-retraining setup and several model classes rather than reproducing the original studies' procedures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own width-sweep outcomes for CIFAR-10 ResNet-20, MNIST networks, linear Gaussian problems, and random-feature regression. Rows below cover reported test-error or test-risk curves and training-error results used to locate interpolation. The paper also reports pruning comparisons, but values visible only in figures are recorded as figure only. It does not sweep training epochs or training-sample counts. Discussion of prior double-descent studies is not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: Its dense-model baselines include a CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 width sweep inspired by Nakkiran et al., and the authors say it shows a test-error peak at the transition to zero training error. They also sweep a two-layer MNIST network. This is a different architecture and recipe from the originals, inside a pruning study. Most rows instead track pruned models at fixed final sparsity against pre-pruning width, which is a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right, but it misses that the novel double descent is for the pruned model at fixed sparsity as pre-pruning size grows. The authors conclude: pruning an overparameterized model can provably beat training the small model, even one given oracle feature locations. Retraining hurts with uncorrelated features but becomes critical as features become correlated. These effects already appear in linear and random-feature models and are verified on neural networks.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines width sweeps followed by pruning to fixed sparsity, often with retraining, and also develops theoretical risk characterizations. It does not reproduce the original model-size, epoch, and sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior differs by setting: double descent is clear in CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 but not clearly visible in the simpler MNIST network; pruning strategy and retraining also change reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed final sparsity, test error of the pruned-and-retrained model plotted against pre-pruning width (or features) shows a double descent. The best result is in the highly overparameterized regime, across ResNet-20, RFR and LGP. The effect is weaker or absent without retraining or with random pruning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning-wise double descent: for a fixed sparsity target, growing the model before pruning gives a second descent in the pruned model's test error past the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: Most curve values are presented only in figures; no numerical curve values or uncertainty estimates are stated in the text. Neural-network results are reported for the described datasets and architectures, and the authors note that double descent is not clearly visible in the MNIST setting.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were kept for sample-size or epoch sweeps because none are reported. Additional pruning comparisons in Figures 5 and 6 are omitted where the text gives no explicit outcome on the width-wise double-descent behavior; the cited random-pruning and no-retraining results are included in r9-r12.

untested.parts: No label-noise variation. Only ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and a two-layer MLP on MNIST, with no uncertainty reported.
Dense LGP and RFR risk curves appear only in figures and are not described in words, so no verdict is given.
No noise or regularization sweep; the authors list regularization as future work.

missing.what: Dense min-norm LGP risk curve risk(β̂) against k/p, with a peak at k=n (n/p=0.3), analytic plus empirical.
Theoretical underparameterized risk σ²/(1−κ), which diverges as p/n→1, plus the overparameterized distributional characterization recovering Hastie et al.'s risk.
Dense RFR curve shape in Fig. 2 (blue), needed to judge V4 in random features.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows concern pruned models, a different construct, and are relinked to none. Only the dense ResNet-20 and MNIST baselines bear on V1, and all values are figure-only. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Only the reported ResNet-20 and two-layer MNIST width sweeps are tested; the study's CIFAR-10 sweep evaluates pruned models at fixed sparsity as well as a dense model.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.
No sweep over training-sample count near an interpolation threshold.
The reported model classes are linear Gaussian problems, random-feature regression, and the studied neural networks; it is not a test across all model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The paper includes noise in its theoretical model but does not report a noise or regularization sweep testing peak dependence, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison of the descent curve with an ordinary U-shaped curve after re-counting effective parameters.
